# App Store Compliance Playbook Catch App Store and Google Play rejection causes before the reviewer does. A reference and a pre-submission guard for iOS and Android apps that is plain about what a scan can prove and what still needs a person. It does not guarantee approval. Read it as a website at [mjmirza.github.io/app-store-compliance](https://mjmirza.github.io/app-store-compliance/). [![Apple App Store](https://img.shields.io/badge/Apple_App_Store-000000?logo=apple&logoColor=white)](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) [![Google Play](https://img.shields.io/badge/Google_Play-414141?logo=googleplay&logoColor=white)](https://play.google/developer-content-policy/) [![Claude Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude_Code-ready-000000?logo=anthropic&logoColor=white)](#how-you-actually-use-this) [![OpenRoots ORA 2.3](https://openroots.org/badge/ora.svg)](https://openroots.org/licenses/ora/2.3) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/ci.yml?branch=main&label=CI)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/actions) [![PRs welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-2ea44f)](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/mjmirza/app-store-compliance?style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/stargazers) [![Forks](https://img.shields.io/github/forks/mjmirza/app-store-compliance?style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/fork) [![Follow mjmirza](https://img.shields.io/github/followers/mjmirza?label=Follow&style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza) **If this saves you even one rejection, leave a star, fork it, and follow along. That is the whole ask.** [Star this repo](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance)  |  [Fork it](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/fork)  |  [Follow on GitHub](https://github.com/mjmirza)  |  [Follow on X](https://twitter.com/MirzaJhanzaib)  |  [next8n.com](https://next8n.com)
## Start here Pick one row. The time shown is for that first step. | You are | Do this first | Time | |---|---|---| | About to submit, and you can open a terminal | Run the two commands below | 2 minutes | | Already rejected | Open [the appeal playbook](docs/MISTAKE-PATTERNS.md#the-appeal-playbook) | 10 minutes | | Not a developer | Open [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md) and do its first two checks | 5 minutes | | Using an AI coding tool (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Grok, Qwen, Kimi and more), and want this on every submit | Go to [the install](#install-it-into-your-ai-coding-tool) | 1 minute | The two commands. Needs git and bash. The first downloads this playbook. The second scans your app. Nothing is installed and nothing in your app is changed. ``` git clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance ~/repositories/app-store-compliance bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/agent-os/hooks/app-store-compliance-guard.sh "/path/to/your/app" ``` Replace only `/path/to/your/app`, with the folder that holds your Xcode project or your Android app. Keep the quotes, they keep a folder name with a space in it whole. To get the path without typing it, drag the folder from Finder or your file manager into the terminal window. A small project scans in about a second, a large one can take up to a minute, and the guard prints the time it took. Findings print first, critical ones on top, each with the file and line that triggered it when there is one. The last lines tell you where you stand. | Verdict line starts with | It means | Do next | |---|---|---| | `BLOCKED.` | A critical rejection risk was found | Fix each `[CRITICAL]` line using the `fix.` line under it, then run the same command again | | `CLEAR.` | No critical risk in your code. Not an approval, the reviewer still checks what a scan cannot see | Do the account and listing checks in [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md), then record them in `.app-review-readiness.json` ([why](docs/WHAT-THE-SCAN-PROVES.md)) | | `Rule pack STALE.` (near the top) | The rules this scan used are more than 60 days old | Update the playbook with `git pull`, then run the scan again | | `NOT CHECKED.` | No iOS or Android project was found in that folder, or the guard could not write its scan files. Run by hand this exits 1. As a hook it lets the command through | Point it at the right folder, and check the temp folder is writable. A managed Expo app with no native folders still gets its `app.json` or `app.config` read for purpose strings, the privacy manifest and Android permissions. Run `npx expo prebuild` to cover the native code too | ## What you get A rejection costs a week. You submit, you wait days in review, you get a one line rejection, you guess at the fix, you resubmit, you wait again. This playbook turns that loop into a check you run before you ever submit. - **You catch the rejection before Apple or Google does.** The guard runs against your project and names the risk while you can still fix it cheaply, not after a reviewer has already said no. - **You stop guessing at the cause.** Every rejection pattern maps to the exact guideline and the exact fix, so a one line rejection email becomes a known problem with a known answer. - **The two checks that cause most rejections are covered first.** A working demo account with a live backend, and a privacy declaration that matches what your app actually does at runtime, including every SDK. These are the top modern rejection causes and the playbook holds them above everything else. - **It works whether or not you write code.** A developer wires the guard into the build. A non developer reads the plain English checklist and walks the submission safely. - **Every claim is real.** Guideline numbers and statistics trace to a live Apple or Google source, never invented, so you are acting on the actual rules, not a guess. It checks that every URL is a real http or https address, that an Apple listing has a support URL, and that a Google listing has a contact email. # ARTEX **Autonomous penetration testing that keeps its receipts.** Self-hosted multi-agent offensive security. A planner explores, workers run real tools, and every finding stays bound to the assets and HTTP traffic that prove it. [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/BaaRai/ARTEX?label=release&color=6b34db)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](LICENSE) [![CI](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Go](https://img.shields.io/github/go-mod/go-version/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](go.mod) [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Screenshots](#screenshots) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#installation) · [Configuration](#configuration) · [Security](SECURITY.md)
--- ARTEX is a self-hosted, LLM-driven penetration testing platform. It is not a chat wrapper around a scanner: a planner splits a goal into intents, workers execute them with real tools, and the results are written back into **two linked graphs**: one for what you know about the target, one for how the test is progressing. Every finding can carry the captured request and response that justify it, and every autonomous action passes through scope rules, approval gates and budgets. - **It explores, it doesn't chat.** Goal decomposition, intent dispatch, worker execution and write-back form a closed loop that keeps advancing until the goal is proven. - **Two graphs, one audit trail.** The shared asset graph says *what exists*; the per-task exploration graph says *what was tried, what it produced, and why*. Anchors link the two. - **Findings with evidence.** A recording MITM proxy and a browser extension capture real traffic; findings, evidence quotes and retests are tied to the exact request/response. - **Autonomy with brakes.** Human-in-the-loop approvals, argv-prefix rules, scope/deny gates, token and turn budgets, a target noise governor, and prompt-injection framing on tool output. - **Self-hosted and model-agnostic.** One Go binary with the Next.js UI embedded, PostgreSQL, your own Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a local Ollama. --- ## Quick start ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD (and optionally an LLM key) docker compose up -d --build # builds from this checkout, starts PostgreSQL ``` Open **http://localhost:8787**. On the first visit `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup: ```bash docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token" ``` > Multi-arch release images (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) are published to GitHub Container > Registry at `ghcr.io/baarai/artex` from the next tagged release; v0.7.0 predates the publish > step. For pulling the prebuilt image and all other installation paths (script, binaries, > source, release archives), see [Installation](#installation). --- ## Multi-provider workers In **System → LLM**, configure the profiles you want to use. In **System → Settings**, set the concurrent worker count to at least **2** before starting a task (the count applies to subsequently started tasks). In **System → Agents → Worker**, leave the model set to follow the task; a fixed Worker model takes precedence over rotation. When creating a task, select both profiles in **LLM config chain**, arrange their order, and enable **Enable multi-LLM worker rotation**. For an existing task, open its LLM config control, change the switch or profile order, and save. Rotation assigns successive worker intents A, B, A, B, regardless of completion order. Separate intents can run concurrently on different providers; each intent keeps its selected provider unless it fails over. Planner and other unbound roles continue using the task's current profile. Turning rotation off restores ordered task-level failover. An excluded provider is skipped, so an intent pinned to an exhausted profile falls back to the task's current profile instead of retrying it; rotation keeps cycling the whole list and does not rebalance around a dead provider. Saving the chain resets their failure state. Changes do not interrupt in-flight calls. The rotation cursor starts again after a server restart and saving the chain does not reset it; the profile order and switch remain persisted. The task creation and `PUT /api/tasks/{id}/llm` APIs accept `llm_rotate: true` alongside the ordered `llm_profile_ids`. Omitting `llm_rotate` on an update preserves its value. ## Screenshots | Tasks | Findings | | :---: | :---: | | ![Tasks](screenshots/tasks.png) | ![Findings](screenshots/findings.png) | | Task execution: sessions and tool calls | Exploration graph | | :---: | :---: | | ![Execution](screenshots/sessions.png) | ![Exploration graph](screenshots/graph.png) | | Asset coverage graph | Traffic recording | | :---: | :---: | | ![Asset coverage graph](screenshots/assets_test.png) | ![Traffic](screenshots/traffic.png) | | Human-in-the-loop chat | Interception approvals | | :---: | :---: | | ![Chat](screenshots/chat.png) | ![Interception](screenshots/intercept.png) |
More screenshots (assets, agents, LLM, logs) | Assets | Agent management | | :---: | :---: | | ![Assets](screenshots/assets.png) | ![Agent](screenshots/agents.png) | | LLM configuration | Backend logs | | :---: | :---: | | ![LLM](screenshots/llm.png) | ![Logs](screenshots/logs.png) |
--- ## How it works ### Dual-graph architecture: exploration graph + asset graph ARTEX separates *what the goals are* from *how far testing has progressed* into two independent graphs linked by anchors: - **Asset graph (shared across tasks).** One source of truth for `root_domain / subdomain / ip / service / app / endpoint`, owned by companies. Parent-child relationships and deduplication keys are computed by the program; agents only submit raw observations. - **Exploration graph (per task).** The task's reasoning and progress: `goal / intent / fact / finding / hint` nodes connected by `spawns / derived_from / yields / proves` edges into a lineage chain. - **Anchors link them.** `exploration_anchors(node_id, asset_id)` ties intents, facts and findings to concrete assets: which assets a direction touched, and which intents tested a given asset. This also powers **asset test coverage** and the coverage graph. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph EG["Exploration graph (per-task · advance chain)"] direction TB G["goal"] I1["intent A"] F1["fact"] I2["intent B"] FD["finding (vulnerability)"] G -->|spawns| I1 I1 -->|yields| F1 F1 -->|derived_from| I2 I2 -->|proves| FD end subgraph AG["Asset graph (globally shared · source of truth)"] direction TB RD["root_domain"] SD["subdomain"] SV["service"] EP["endpoint"] RD --> SD --> SV --> EP end I1 -. anchor .-> SD F1 -. anchor .-> SV I2 -. anchor .-> EP FD -. anchor .-> EP ``` The **planner** reads the exploration graph, judges goals, and dispatches intents only when there is an uncovered direction; a **worker** claims one intent, executes it, writes assets/facts/findings back into both graphs, then stops. ### The engine loop The engine is event-driven: any graph change wakes the planner, workers claim and execute intents, write-back triggers the next round, until `prove_goal` closes the task. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant EV as graph-change debounce participant P as planner participant FR as frontier intent queue participant W as worker participant PX as recording proxy participant DB as dual graphs + activity EV-->>P: wake up P->>DB: read situation (graph_overview prefetch + coverage/scope) P->>FR: dispatch 0..N intents (with asset_ids) Note over P,FR: most wake-ups dispatch 0 (no new direction means done) W->>FR: claimNext claims one intent W->>DB: fetch the raw assets of the intent's asset_ids W->>PX: real tool execution (Kali / Bash / HTTP) PX-->>W: response (fully traced + CA verified) W->>DB: write back fact / asset / finding + per-step activity DB-->>EV: graph change EV-->>P: wake again (closed loop) ``` ### Durable attack chains, shared worker memory Real attack chains are multi-step and ordered (find an injection → get credentials → move laterally). The planner keeps a **todolist retained per task across wake-ups**: it records the chain once, then dispatches the next step only when its prerequisites are satisfied by facts. Workers can also **search each other's execution traces** (`search_all_worker_traces`, `list_worker_traces`, `get_worker_trace`). Observations that never became formal facts (an error message, a response snippet, a hidden parameter) are still reusable by the next worker, while each worker remains confined to the intent it claimed. --- ## Features ### Evidence, not chat logs - **Recording MITM proxy** (`:8788`) with a generated CA: every Bash/HTTP tool call is traced, and request/response evidence can be bound to a finding. - **Browser extension** (`extension/`) for authenticated targets: log in once (captcha, email OTP, 2FA included), capture the session, and the requests/responses land in the same traffic store.
Using the traffic capture extension - Load the unpacked extension from `extension/` (Chrome/Edge: Developer Mode → Load unpacked); - In the popup, set your ARTEX URL and token, then press **Start capture** on the tab you are browsing; - Use the site normally; text requests/responses are batched to `POST /api/traffic/ingest` (authenticated). Binary bodies (images, fonts) are skipped, bodies are truncated at 256 KiB, batches are capped at 50 entries; - Press **Stop** when done. Everything stays in your local traffic store.
- **Verified findings**: findings carry a POE level, a verification status and a note; a finding is `verified` only when a bound proof/response and verbatim evidence quotes support it. Gzip/deflate bodies are decoded before the quote check. The findings table supports bulk status updates, and the report and export show each finding's proof strength next to its status. - **Traffic replay**: open a captured exchange and replay the recorded request (method, URL, headers and stored body) from the traffic detail; replay stays disabled while only the body preview is loaded. - **Vulnerability retest loop**: a dedicated `retester` agent re-runs a finding with optional fixed version/conditions, records `Still reproducible / Fixed / Cannot confirm`, and can move the finding to `Fixed` automatically. Original evidence and reports are preserved. - **Reports and exports**: findings, evidence and task archives, with traffic snapshots kept encrypted at rest. ### Control without slowing down - **Interception gate**: every tool call can require human approval, with rules by `string`, `regex` or **argv prefix**. An argv rule is a JSON array of 1 to 8 tokens (Bash only, for example `["git","push"]`); it matches only a single simple command whose parsed prefix equals the pattern exactly. Pipes, lists, redirections, prefix assignments, subshells, background jobs, wrapper programs and command/parameter substitutions do not match; flags are ignored by construction (`["git","push"]` covers `git push --force`, but `git -C /repo push` matches nothing). Each approval records who decided: `human`, `rule`, `model` or `system`. - **Scope and target gate**: scope rows define the coverage denominator; assets outside the declared scope are not explored. The target gate (off by default, API-only) can refuse destinations that were not approved. - **Budgets**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a whole task (planner and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Near the limit the task enters a forced wrap-up; a worker is not started when the remaining budget cannot cover it. Spend already in `llm_usage` is restored after a restart. A task that is already inside the wrap-up reserve only has that reserve left, so the revived run wraps up instead of starting another worker. The per-worker cost estimate starts again from the defaults (50,000 tokens and 10 turns) until a worker finishes in this process. - **Noise governor**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE=quiet|balanced|aggressive` paces requests ARTEX sends to targets (per-host rate, burst, in-flight limit, jitter, backoff on 429/503, short GET caching). With a profile set, agents also receive low-and-slow flags for the installed scanners. - **Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Disable with `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0`. ### Assets and coverage - **Coverage ledger and force-directed coverage graph**: in-scope assets are highlighted as tested or untested, with linked intents, facts and findings per node. - **Company-scoped asset graph**: shared across tasks, deduplicated by the program, with domain → subdomain → service → endpoint containment. - **ScopeSentry sync**: pull asset data from a [ScopeSentry](https://github.com/Autumn-27/ScopeSentry) instance by project or task, merged by company scope into the asset graph for agents to explore.
Syncing from ScopeSentry - On the **Asset Sync** page, enter the ScopeSentry address and API key; - Choose the targets and asset types by **project** or **task** (domains / subdomains / IPs / ports / sites / endpoints…); - Import: rows are merged by company asset scope and become part of the asset graph.
- **Task categories, templates, relations and archives** for repeatable engagements. ### Platform - **LLM profiles with failover**: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible relays and keyless Ollama; multiple profiles per task with automatic failover. - **Token accounting**: per-task and per-session usage, cache reads/writes, and an LLM record view for every call. - **MCP servers, skills, memory and a workspace**: extend the agent with remote tools and reusable prompt/playbook material. - **Web search**: the agent's search tool uses Brave, Tavily or the opt-in Keenable backend, configured in **System → Settings** with the key encrypted at rest; search can also egress through its own proxy. - **Single binary**: the Next.js UI is embedded with `go:embed`; PostgreSQL is the only external dependency. --- ## Installation > Requires **PostgreSQL**; exploration requires an **LLM** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or > `OPENAI_API_KEY`, also configurable in the UI). ### Option 1: one-click install script (recommended) ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX ./install.sh ``` The script detects or installs Docker, then offers **① all-Docker** (writes `.env`, runs `docker compose up -d --build`) or **② local build and run** (generates `config.json`, builds the embedded binary, starts it). Open **http://localhost:8787**; `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup (`docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token"`). The UI listens on `127.0.0.1` by default. To reach it from another machine (or from Windows when ARTEX runs inside WSL), set `ARTEX_BIND_ADDR=0.0.0.0` in `.env` (the setup token still protects the first-run claim), or keep loopback and use a reverse proxy or SSH tunnel. ### Option 2: Docker (Compose checkout build or prebuilt GHCR image) Build from a checkout with Docker Compose: ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD, optionally ANTHROPIC_API_KEY docker compose up -d --build # → http://localhost:8787 ``` The release workflow publishes a multi-arch image (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) to GitHub Container Registry on each `v*` tag, with tags `:latest`, `:v`, and `:`. v0.7.0 predates that step, so there is no `artex` package yet: until the next tagged release, use the checkout build above, and `docker-compose.ghcr.yml` and the `docker pull` below will fail with `denied`. GHCR packages start private; after the first publish the package visibility must be set to Public, and the release workflow verifies that the image pulls anonymously and fails the job otherwise. Once the image is published, the standalone container requires an existing PostgreSQL database reachable from the container. Set the `ARTEX_PG_*` variables below. The example uses Docker Desktop's `host.docker.internal` to reach PostgreSQL on the host. On native Linux Docker Engine, add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to `docker run` for a host database, or use the reachable hostname of your database server. ```bash docker pull ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest mkdir -p data keys docker run -d --name artex \ --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \ -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 \ -p 127.0.0.1:8788:8788 \ -e ARTEX_PG_HOST=host.docker.internal \ -e ARTEX_PG_PORT=5432 \ -e ARTEX_PG_USER=artex \ -e ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD='yourpass' \ -e ARTEX_PG_DBNAME=artex \ -e ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE=disable \ -e ARTEX_JWT_KEY_DIR=/app/keys \ -v "$PWD/data:/app/data" \ -v "$PWD/keys:/app/keys" \ ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest # → http://localhost:8787 (docker logs artex | grep "Setup token") ``` In `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.ghcr.yml`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is passed to ARTEX as its own variable. The server percent-encodes it into the connection URL, so a password may contain `/`, `?`, `%`, `@`, `:` or spaces. In `.env`, quote a value that contains `#`, and write `$$` for a literal `$`. The `ARTEX_PG_*` variables take the password raw; quote it in a shell. The image includes a scanner toolchain (`nmap`, `nuclei`, `httpx`, `katana`, `ffuf`, `dalfox`, `sqlmap`, `ripgrep`, `curl`, `npm`, …) and built-in `/app/skills`. The GHCR Compose file below persists `./keys` and `./data`; it does not mount a host `skills/` directory, so the image's built-in skills are used. #### Compose stack from the prebuilt image `docker-compose.ghcr.yml` runs the same ARTEX + PostgreSQL stack from the released image, with no checkout build. The image is not published yet: v0.7.0 predates the GHCR publish step, so use the checkout build above until the next tagged release. Once the first image is published, download the file and `.env.example` once: ```bash curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/main/docker-compose.ghcr.yml curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/main/.env.example cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD, optionally an LLM key docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml pull docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up -d # → http://localhost:8787 (docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml logs artex | grep "Setup token") ``` Update the stack without a git checkout: ```bash docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml pull docker compose -f docker-compose.ghcr.yml up -d ``` Pin a version with `ARTEX_IMAGE_TAG=v0.7.1` in `.env` (or `0.7.1`); unset uses `latest`. To use custom skills, copy them into a host directory and add `- ./skills:/app/skills` to the `artex` volumes, which overrides the built-in `/app/skills`. For remote MCP you can choose `http` (Streamable HTTP) or `sse` (legacy SSE) in system settings. Legacy SSE servers usually establish the event stream with `GET /sse` and receive JSON-RPC over `/message?sessionId=...`; configure the URL as `/sse` and send `Authorization: Bearer `. ### Option 3: prebuilt binaries (Releases) Download the zip for your platform from [Releases](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases). It contains `artex`, `start.sh` (`start.bat` on Windows), `skills/` and `config.example.json`: ```bash cp config.example.json config.json # fill in the database connection ./start.sh # → http://localhost:8787 ``` Start with `start.sh` / `start.bat`, not `./artex`: it is a daemon script that restarts the process after a backoff. To keep it in the background: `nohup ./start.sh >artex.log 2>&1 &`. #### Verifying a release Each release attaches `SHA256SUMS` and a CycloneDX SBOM, `artex-.cdx.json` (Go modules in the linux/amd64 binary, the frontend `package-lock.json`, `go.mod`/`go.sum`), next to the zips. The zips also carry a GitHub build provenance attestation. Releases published before this was added have neither. ```bash sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS # add --ignore-missing if you downloaded only some zips gh attestation verify --repo BaaRai/ARTEX # built by this repository's release workflow ``` ### Option 4: build the single binary from source ```bash cd web && npm ci && npm run build:static && cd .. cp -r web/out server/webui/dist CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags embedui -o artex ./cmd/artex ./start.sh ``` Only `-tags embedui` embeds the frontend into the binary. ### Option 5: cross-platform release archives `build.sh` builds and embeds the frontend, strips debug info, and writes zips for Linux amd64/arm64, macOS amd64/arm64 and Windows amd64 by default: ```bash ./build.sh --release # output: dist/artex--*.zip ARTEX_TARGETS=linux/amd64,windows/amd64 ./build.sh --release ./build.sh --target linux/amd64 --upx ``` UPX is disabled by default: self-extracting binaries may be incompatible with some kernels, virtualization environments or security policies. ARTEX adds `/model/{model}/invoke` (or `/invoke-with-response-stream`), sends `anthropic_version: bedrock-2023-05-31`, and decodes Bedrock's binary event stream. Enter the model ID manually; this gateway format does not have a model-list operation. The token and custom header values are encrypted in the database and are write-only in the UI. Editing the gateway URL requires re-entering the token, so saved credentials cannot be sent to a different host by changing the URL. This format is for bearer-authenticated gateways; direct AWS Bedrock with SigV4 credentials is not supported. For environment-based setup, set `ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER=bedrock-gateway`, `ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL`, `ARTEX_LLM_MODEL`, and `ARTEX_LLM_API_KEY`. Optional `ARTEX_LLM_CUSTOM_HEADERS` uses the same newline-separated `Name: Value` format. **Task archive storage**: local disk by default. Set `ARTEX_ARCHIVE_STORAGE=s3` to store cold task packages in an S3-compatible bucket and release their local package space after verification. Existing local archives remain usable. See [Task archive storage](docs/task-archive-storage.md) for configuration, permissions, integrity checks, temporary disk requirements and recovery. **Concurrency**: work agents per task, in "System Settings" (default 3). **Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results for the worker, planner, chat and main agent are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Unset or empty, the boundary is on; set `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0` (or `false` / `off` / `no`) to disable it. Cost: about 154 bytes per tool result plus one system note. **Noise profile (off by default)**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE` paces the requests ARTEX sends to targets (WebFetch, HTTP custom tools, the enrich probe). Unset or `off` keeps today's behaviour: no limit, no cache. `quiet` = 2 req/s per host (burst 4, 1 in flight), `balanced` = 5 req/s (burst 10, 2 in flight), `aggressive` = 20 req/s (burst 40, 4 in flight). A profile adds jitter, backs off on 429/503 (honours `Retry-After`, bounded retries, GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only), deduplicates identical in-flight GETs and caches them briefly (60/30/10 s; never POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), and logs a per-host noise line each minute. `ARTEX_TARGET_USER_AGENT` sets a User-Agent on target requests that carry none. With traffic capture on, Bash commands that use the proxy (curl, wget, python-requests) are paced too, per host by the same rate and jitter, and counted in the same per-host lines. The in-flight caps, retries and cache apply only to ARTEX's own requests. This is best effort, not a security boundary. Raw scanners such as nmap are not paced, and neither is a command that bypasses the proxy (`--noproxy`, a removed proxy variable). With capture off, nothing launched from Bash is paced. The low-and-slow prompt block supplies the rate flags in every case. The **Target noise** card in System settings sets the profile at runtime (no restart) and shows the per-host counters; once saved, that setting takes precedence over `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE`. **Scanner User-Agent (opt-in per task)** adds a stable ARTEX User-Agent to supported target requests so defenders can correlate them with an approved assessment. See the [configuration and WAF triage guide](docs/scanner-user-agent.md). **Low-and-slow agent guidance (off by default)**: when a noise profile is set, the planner, worker, main agent and chat agents receive a code-owned prompt block with the profile's per-host limits and exact rate/delay flags for the installed scanners. It tells them to test one host at a time, back off on 429/503 and never raise the rate to meet a deadline. **Run budgets (off by default)**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a task's total spend (planner rounds and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Unset or `0` means unlimited. A worker is not started when the remaining task budget cannot cover its estimated cost (the average of finished workers, else 50,000 tokens and 10 turns). Near the wrap-up reserve (the larger of 5% and 20,000 tokens, and 2 turns) the task enters a forced wrap-up: the planner writes a summary and final goal judgment, and workers may only write back. The task then ends `done` if its goals are met, else `timeout`. Practical floor: below 50,000 tokens no worker starts; 50,000-70,000 typically gives one worker then wrap-up; pick well above 70,000 for real exploration. Planner, worker, judge, and compactor rows in `llm_usage` are counted back into the cap when a ledger is created, including after a restart and after a revived run drops its ledger. A restored task already inside the wrap-up reserve does not get another worker: only that reserve remains, and the run wraps up. Chat, goal decomposition, and side questions are stored on the same task and are not counted. The per-worker average is not restored (usage rows have no run boundary), so the estimate starts from the defaults until a worker finishes in this process. **Common flags**: `./start.sh -addr :8787 -proxy :8788` (`-addr` frontend/API, `-proxy` traffic recording proxy). ### External PostgreSQL ARTEX already supports an external PostgreSQL 16+ instance — the `postgres` service in `docker-compose.yml` is only the bundled default. Because the database is startup configuration and the system's single source of truth, there is no runtime database switcher in the UI: change the environment variables and restart the server to point at another instance. Configure the connection with either a full connection string or individual parts: - **`ARTEX_PG_DSN`**: full PostgreSQL connection URL (for example `postgres://artex:pass@db.example.internal:5432/artex?sslmode=require`). When set, it takes precedence over the `ARTEX_PG_*` variables and you are responsible for percent-encoding any URL-special characters in the username or password. - **`ARTEX_PG_*` parts** (recommended when passwords contain `/`, `?`, `%`, `@`, `:`, or spaces — ARTEX percent-encodes the user and password and removes `ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD` from the environment at startup): - `ARTEX_PG_HOST` — PostgreSQL host - `ARTEX_PG_PORT` — PostgreSQL port (default `5432`) - `ARTEX_PG_USER` — database user - `ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD` — database password (raw, not URL-encoded) - `ARTEX_PG_DBNAME` — database name - `ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE` — TLS mode (`disable`, `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`) #### Compose without the bundled `postgres` service To run ARTEX against an external PostgreSQL server with Docker Compose, remove the `postgres` service, the `depends_on` block, and the `pgdata` volume from `docker-compose.yml`, and point `artex` at your database: ```yaml services: artex: image: ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest security_opt: - "no-new-privileges:true" environment: # Option A: individual parts (recommended; percent-encodes special characters) ARTEX_PG_HOST: ${ARTEX_PG_HOST:?Set ARTEX_PG_HOST in .env} ARTEX_PG_PORT: ${ARTEX_PG_PORT:-5432} ARTEX_PG_USER: ${ARTEX_PG_USER:-artex} ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD: ${ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD:?Set ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD in .env} ARTEX_PG_DBNAME: ${ARTEX_PG_DBNAME:-artex} ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE: ${ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE:-require} # Option B: full DSN (overrides ARTEX_PG_* when set) # ARTEX_PG_DSN: ${ARTEX_PG_DSN} ARTEX_JWT_KEY_DIR: /app/keys ports: - "${ARTEX_BIND_ADDR:-127.0.0.1}:8787:8787" - "127.0.0.1:8788:8788" volumes: - ./data:/app/data - ./keys:/app/keys restart: unless-stopped ``` #### Local disk usage (`data/`) Moving PostgreSQL to an external host does **not** move the runtime `data/` directory off local disk. `data/` still stores spilled HTTP/TCP traffic blobs (`data/traffic/_blobs`), LLM transcripts, task working files, and local task archives, so heavy workloads can still fill the host disk if `data/` is on a small volume. Mount `data/` on a suitably sized volume, and consider setting `ARTEX_ARCHIVE_STORAGE=s3` (see [Task archive storage](docs/task-archive-storage.md)) to offload cold task archives to object storage. ### Reverse proxy deployment (HTTPS / exposing only 443) The frontend, API and SSE stream share port 8787 (the binary listens on `127.0.0.1:8787` by default; the Docker container publishes on `127.0.0.1`), and the activity stream is same-origin by default, so **no `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` is needed**: expose 443 and keep 8787 internal. SSE keeps a long-lived connection with continuous pushes, so the proxy **must disable buffering**; otherwise the browser connects but never receives events. Redirect plain HTTP first, so a bookmarked `http://` URL never reaches the app unencrypted: ```nginx server { listen 80; server_name your.domain.com; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } ``` Then the TLS server: ```nginx server { listen 443 ssl; server_name your.domain.com; # ssl_certificate / ssl_certificate_key ... location / { # 512 MiB combined file limit plus 1 MiB of multipart metadata. client_max_body_size 513m; proxy_request_buffering off; proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; # SSE essentials: buffering off, long timeouts, HTTP/1.1 proxy_buffering off; proxy_cache off; proxy_read_timeout 3600s; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection ""; } } ``` **Login rate limit behind a proxy**: login allows 10 attempts per minute per client IP. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address, so without further setup all users share one budget and an attacker who fails 10 logins blocks everyone, admin included, for up to 15 minutes. Keep the `X-Forwarded-For` line and set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (comma-separated CIDRs, empty by default) to the address ARTEX sees the proxy connect from: - **nginx and ARTEX both on the host** (binary, `./start.sh`): the peer is `127.0.0.1`; start ARTEX with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1/32`. - **nginx on the host, ARTEX in Docker** (`docker-compose.yml`): the connection reaches the container from the Docker bridge gateway (a `172.x` address), not from `127.0.0.1`. Find it with `docker network inspect artex_default --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}'` (the network is `_default`), put `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=/32` in `.env`, then `docker compose up -d`. For a peer in that list, ARTEX reads `X-Forwarded-For` from the right and takes the first address that is not a trusted proxy; from any other peer the header is ignored. Trust only proxies you run: a trusted peer can claim any client address. **Security headers**: every response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a same-origin referrer policy and a `frame-ancestors 'self'` CSP; console documents additionally get a `Permissions-Policy` and COOP/CORP. `Strict-Transport-Security` is sent only when the request is known to be HTTPS: directly over TLS, or via `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` from a trusted proxy. The same list above enables it, so with nginx in front, the 443 server answers with HSTS after you set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES`. > Only when SSE needs a different origin from the page (e.g. a dedicated subdomain) should you set > `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` **at build time** (it is baked into the static bundle during `next build`; > setting it at container runtime has no effect). --- ## Operations ### Troubleshooting an empty tool call In the task's session transcript, expand the affected tool call and compare **Command** and **Output**. The `UNTRUSTED_OUTPUT` markers identify the boundary around tool output. They are expected and should stay enabled while troubleshooting. - **Command shows `{}`.** The recorded tool input is an empty JSON object. For a tool that requires a command, this means its command argument was missing. Check which model and version produced the call. - **Command shows `(empty)` or `(failed to load)`.** The transcript has no input detail to display or could not fetch it. If the session record contains a command, include that discrepancy in a report. - **Output shows `[]`.** This is the recorded result body. Check the row's success or failure indicator and its input separately before drawing conclusions about what ran. For a recurring problem, share the ARTEX version or commit, the model and version, and a sanitized excerpt of the affected input and result. Remove credentials, target data, and other sensitive content before sharing. ### Backups `scripts/backup.sh` dumps the Postgres database (and optionally the data directory) with timestamped output and rotation: ```bash scripts/backup.sh --with-data # db dump + data/ archive, keep 14 scripts/backup.sh --keep 7 # db only, keep 7 ``` Restore into a running stack: ```bash gunzip -c backups/artex-db-.sql.gz | docker compose exec -T postgres \ psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" ``` Stored secrets (LLM API keys, proxies and gateway custom headers, MCP env, task credentials, notification channel config, Brave/Tavily search keys, web search and global proxies, the execution spec of custom tools, the capture-proxy rewrite rules) are encrypted in the database with the key in `keys/secret.key` (generated at first start, mode 0600, next to `jwt.key`). **A database backup without that key cannot restore those secrets**: back up `keys/` with the dump, separately. Deployments without a persistent disk set `ARTEX_SECRET_KEY` (32 bytes, base64 or hex, e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`). ARTEX refuses to start when the database holds encrypted secrets and no key is available. Daily cron example (03:20, operator crontab): ``` 20 3 * * * cd /path/to/ARTEX && scripts/backup.sh --with-data >> backups/backup.log 2>&1 ``` ### Updating and upgrading > Upgrading swaps the program and never touches data: the Postgres volume `pgdata`, `./data` > (traffic index, task files, transcripts), `./keys` (`jwt.key`, `secret.key`) and `./skills` are > preserved. **No manual database step is needed**: on every start ARTEX applies its embedded > `schema.sql` baseline, then any pending numbered migration from `db/migrations/`, in order, each > in its own transaction. Restarting the new binary is the upgrade. Back up `./data`, `keys/` and > the database before upgrading. **Update banner (opt-in, off by default)**: start ARTEX with `ARTEX_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to ask the public GitHub releases API for the latest tag, at most once per 24 hours (cached in memory; a failed check is not retried within that window). When the release is newer, the web UI shows a dismissible strip linking to Releases. The request sends only `User-Agent: artex-update-check`. Unset, ARTEX makes no update request and shows no banner. #### Upgrading from a clone made before 2026-10-23 The repository history was rewritten that day to drop a personal email address from the commit metadata. Agent capabilities come from the [`norma`](https://github.com/Autumn-27/norma) SDK (`agentcore` / `tool` / `permission` / `harness` / `memory` / `transcript`). At its core is the **dual-graph architecture**, plus two autonomy mechanisms: **process-level information exchange between workers** and the **planner's multi-round shared todolist**. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph FE["Frontend Next.js (go:embed embedded single binary)"] UI["Dashboard · Tasks · Assets · Coverage graph · Traffic · Workspace · System settings"] end subgraph SRV["server (Go net/http)"] API["REST /api/* JWT auth SSE"] ENG["engine scheduling loop"] MGR["Manager task/engine/store lifecycle"] end subgraph AG["agent (norma SDK)"] GO["goals goal decomposition + scope extraction"] PL["planner the planner (sole intent generator)"] WK["worker executor ×N"] MA["mainagent human-in-the-loop"] end subgraph DB["PostgreSQL"] AGRAPH["Asset graph assets / companies / task_scope"] EGRAPH["Exploration graph exploration_nodes / anchors / activity"] end subgraph SUB["Supporting subsystems"] PROXY["Traffic recording proxy MITM + CA tracing"] GUARD["guard / intercept tool approval gate"] ENR["enrich DNS / HTTP async enrichment"] EXT["MCP · skills · memory · report"] end UI -->|HTTP| API API --> MGR --> ENG ENG --> PL ENG --> WK API --> MA API --> GO PL --> DB WK --> DB MA --> DB GO --> DB WK -->|"Bash / HTTP fully traced"| PROXY WK --> GUARD WK --> ENR PL -.-> EXT WK -.-> EXT MA -.-> EXT ``` | Layer | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | **Frontend** | Next.js static export embedded via `go:embed`; Operational security properties: - **Secrets at rest**: LLM keys/proxies/gateway headers, MCP environment, task credentials, notification config, search keys, proxies, custom-tool execution specs, capture-proxy rewrite rules and traffic evidence snapshots are encrypted with AES-256-GCM using `keys/secret.key` (or `ARTEX_SECRET_KEY`). ARTEX refuses to start when encrypted data exists and no usable key is available. - **First-run claim**: `/setup` requires a one-time token printed at startup; the UI binds to `127.0.0.1` by default. - **Login protection**: 10 attempts per minute per client IP, with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` for correct client attribution behind a reverse proxy. - **Untrusted tool output**: framed as data for every agent by default (prompt-injection boundary). - **Release integrity**: SHA-256 sums, CycloneDX SBOM and GitHub build provenance attestations for release archives. --- ## About this fork This repository is the English translation and continuation of ARTEX, originally by [Autumn-27](https://github.com/Autumn-27).
